old: Its distant root simply meant 'to raise up' — the same lifting motion behind a very common English verb.
It once named nothing more than a small bud or shoot, before it came to mean growing rapidly.
One theory ties it to Latin burra, 'wool' or 'fluff,' perhaps for the fuzzy coat on certain young buds.
clues: This verb describing a kind of increase began life as a noun that simply named a small bud or shoot on a plant.
It means more than just growing: to expand quickly and vigorously, flourishing the way a city's population or a young industry suddenly booms.
You often see it describing something that is thriving, as in "a ____ art scene," and it shares an ancient root meaning "to raise up" with the word "bear."
